item.title: Instruction Set Architectures
item.description: As software engineers, we absolutely love building and using abstractions. Just imagine how much stuff happens when you load a URL. You type something on a keyboard; key presses are somehow detected by the OS and get sent to the browser; browser parses the URL and asks the OS to make a network request; then comes DNS, routing, TCP, HTTP, and all the other OSI layers; browser parses HTML; JavaScript works its magic; some representation of a page gets sent over to GPU for rendering; image frames get sent to the monitor… and each of these steps probably involves doing dozens of more specific things in the process.

item.title: Assembly Language
item.description: CPUs are controlled with machine language, which is just a stream of binary-encoded instructions that specify the instruction number (called opcode), what its operands are (if there are any), and where to store the result (if one is produced). A much more human-friendly rendition of machine language, called assembly language, uses mnemonic codes to refer to machine code instructions and symbolic names to refer to registers and other storage locations.

item.title: Loops and Conditionals
item.description: Let’s consider a slightly more complex example: loop: add edx, DWORD PTR [rax] add rax, 4 cmp rax, rcx jne loop It calculates the sum of a 32-bit integer array, just as a simple for loop would. The “body” of the loop is add edx, DWORD PTR [rax]: this instruction loads data from the iterator rax and adds it to the accumulator edx. Next, we move the iterator 4 bytes forward with add rax, 4.

item.title: Functions and Recursion
item.description: At the machine-code level, calling a function is mostly a jump with a return address attached. The difficult part is not getting there. It is agreeing on what the registers and stack mean when we arrive. Suppose one compilation unit calls a function from a library that was compiled last year. The caller does not know which registers the function uses internally, how much temporary storage it needs, or whether it calls another function.

item.title: Indirect Branching
item.description: A normal branch says where it is going in its own machine code. An indirect branch takes the destination from a register or memory location: jmp rax call QWORD PTR [rdi] This small difference lets us implement switch tables, function pointers, interpreters, and runtime polymorphism. It also creates a harder prediction problem: the processor must guess not only whether a branch is taken, but which of many possible addresses comes next.

item.title: Machine Code Layout
item.description: Computer engineers like to mentally split the pipeline of a CPU into two parts: the front-end, where instructions are fetched from memory and decoded, and the back-end, where they are scheduled and finally executed. Typically, the performance is bottlenecked by the execution stage, and for this reason, most of our efforts in this book are going to be spent towards optimizing around the back-end. But sometimes the reverse can happen when the front-end doesn’t feed instructions to the back-end fast enough to saturate it.

item.title: Interrupts and System Calls
item.description: Our assembly programs have so far lived in an unusually peaceful universe. They read and write memory, perform arithmetic, and eventually return. Real programs also need to open files, allocate pages, receive network packets, and occasionally discover that the user has pressed a key. The CPU cannot let an arbitrary program control these facilities directly. A process that could rewrite page tables or talk to a storage controller could inspect or destroy every other process on the machine.

item.title: Virtualization
item.description: An operating system kernel is written under the reasonable assumption that it controls the machine. A virtual machine lets several kernels maintain this belief at the same time. The software making this possible is a virtual-machine monitor, more commonly called a hypervisor. It presents each guest with virtual CPUs, memory, interrupts, and devices while retaining control of the physical versions. The difficult part is not imitating add: ordinary arithmetic already has exactly the behavior the guest expects.
